howToUse: This script bank gives you the exact words for three conversations that will happen before your niche is finalised — and that will derail you if you don't have a ready answer. Pull up the relevant script the moment the situation arises: use it word-for-word, or read it once to anchor your thinking before you speak. You do not need to adapt it — it is already written for your situation.
promise: Use these scripts to move through the three conversations that stop most women from starting — without waiting for your niche to be finished first. Every sentence is already written; your only job is to say it.

tools.name: The Inner Doubt Script — What to Say to Yourself When 'I Need to Finalise My Niche First' Surfaces
tools.instructions: Read this out loud — or write it in your journal — the moment you catch yourself using niche uncertainty as a reason to wait. Use it as written.
tools.content:
## When the thought appears: *"I'm not ready to start because I haven't figured out my niche yet"*

---

### What is actually happening right now

The thought feels logical. It sounds responsible. *Get clear first, then move.* The problem is that this particular kind of clarity — the kind that tells you exactly which slice of your expertise is a sellable consulting offer versus background knowledge people assume is free — cannot be produced by sitting alone with a notes app. It is produced by a specific process applied to your specific career history. Which means waiting for the niche to arrive before you start is the same as waiting for the destination to appear before you get in the car.

The doubt is not a signal that you need more time. It is a signal that you are about to do something that matters.

---

### Say this to yourself — word for word

**Step 1 — Name what is happening:**
> *"I notice I'm using niche uncertainty as a reason not to move. That is a holding pattern, not a preparation phase."*

**Step 2 — Separate the feeling from the fact:**
> *"Not having a finalised niche right now is not evidence that I can't get one. It is evidence that I haven't yet done the specific work that produces one. Those are completely different things."*

**Step 3 — Name what is actually true about you:**
> *"I have [NUMBER] years of professional experience in [YOUR FORMER FIELD — e.g., financial services / HR / healthcare operations / communications]. That expertise already exists. It is not something I need to build. I need to identify which part of it is a consulting offer — and that is a process, not a personality trait."*

**Step 4 — Close the loop:**
> *"The notes app is not going to tell me. A structured process applied to my actual career history will. My job right now is not to figure out the niche. My job is to do the work that figures it out."*

---

### If the doubt comes back within the hour

It will. Say this:

> *"I've already answered this. The answer hasn't changed. The discomfort is not new information."*

Then do the next concrete action in your programme — not more research, not more note-taking. The next action.

tools.name: The Partner / Spouse Script — What to Say When Asked 'Are You Sure About This Yet?'
tools.instructions: Use this before or during the conversation with a partner or spouse who is asking — with care or with scepticism — whether you have your niche figured out. Read it once before the conversation so the shape of it is in your head, or use the direct quotes word-for-word.
tools.content:
## The conversation: your partner asks whether you've figured out what you're doing yet

This conversation tends to happen at the kitchen table, usually in the evening, usually when you've just opened the laptop and they've noticed. It is not an attack. It is often genuine concern dressed up as a practical question. But if you answer it in the way the question is framed — *yes I have* or *not quite yet* — you put yourself in a position where your progress is measured by whether you can name a finished niche on demand. That is the wrong measure.

---

### The reframe you need before you speak

The question *"are you sure about your niche yet?"* assumes that the niche is something you figure out before you start, the way you pick a destination before a road trip. The process you are working through is built on the opposite logic: the consulting offer is identified *through* structured work on your actual career history, not decided in advance of it. You don't need to defend that. You need to explain it once, clearly, so they understand what "progress" actually looks like.

---

### Say this — word for word if you need to

**Opening — acknowledge the question without accepting its frame:**
> *"I know it looks like I'm still in the 'figuring it out' stage, and I want to explain what's actually happening — because I think the way this works is different from what either of us assumed."*

**The explanation — one short paragraph:**
> *"The reason I haven't named a specific niche yet isn't that I'm uncertain or avoiding it. It's that identifying which part of my [FORMER FIELD — e.g., project management / compliance / marketing] background is a real consulting offer — versus just professional experience people assume is free — requires a specific process. That process is what I'm working through right now. The niche comes out of the work, not before it."*

**The concrete anchor — give them something to hold:**
> *"Here's what I can tell you with certainty: I'm working in [FORMER FIELD]. I'm building toward [DESCRIBE THE CLIENT TYPE — e.g., 'helping mid-size businesses with the kind of regulatory process work I spent eight years doing' / 'working with teams going through the kind of organisational change I led three times']. The specific framing will be sharper in [REALISTIC TIMEFRAME — e.g., 'the next three to four weeks'] once I've done the excavation work."*

**If they push — if the question becomes 'but what if you go through all this and it turns out there's no market?':**
> *"That's actually the right question, and it's one the process is designed to answer. I'm not going to commit to a niche and then find out no one pays for it. I'm going to identify what the market in my field actually pays for first — and build the offer from that. That's the opposite of guessing."*

**The close — what you need from them:**
> *"What I need from you right now isn't certainty from me. It's a bit of room to do the work without having to be able to summarise it every time you ask. Can you give me [TIMEFRAME — e.g., four weeks / until the end of the month] before we do a proper check-in on where things stand?"*

---

### After the conversation

Write down the date of the check-in you agreed to. Put it somewhere you both see it. This moves the conversation from open-ended anxiety to a named moment — which is much easier for everyone to hold.

tools.name: The Network Conversation Script — What to Say When Someone Asks 'So What Are You Doing Now?'
tools.instructions: Use this in any first-contact or reconnection conversation — coffee, a LinkedIn message exchange, a chance meeting — before you have a polished niche statement. This replaces 'I'm still figuring it out' with a sentence that is honest, confident, and invites the right follow-up.
tools.content:
## The situation: someone asks what you're working on and your niche isn't finished yet

This is the conversation most women avoid entirely — or stumble through — because the honest answer (*"I'm still figuring out my niche"*) sounds unconfident, and a made-up polished answer feels like a lie. Neither serves you. There is a third option: a true, confident sentence that describes what you are building toward without requiring the niche to be complete.

---

### The shape of a strong pre-niche answer

A strong answer does three things: it names your former field so the person knows your ground, it names the direction you're moving so they know this is active not exploratory, and it opens the door to their input so the conversation becomes useful rather than performative.

You do not need to say "consulting" if it feels premature. You do not need to name a niche you haven't confirmed. You need one honest sentence and one opening question.

---

### The core script — use as written or adapt the fields

**When the question is casual — 'so what are you up to these days?'**

> *"I spent [NUMBER] years in [FORMER FIELD — e.g., supply chain / talent development / commercial finance] before I stepped back when my kids were young. They're older now, and I'm building a consulting practice — I'm currently working out exactly which part of that [FORMER FIELD] work is the most useful to bring to clients first. I'd actually love to hear what you're seeing in that space — are you still working in [THEIR FIELD / RELEVANT CONTEXT]?"*

---

**When the question is more direct — 'what kind of consulting?'**

> *"My background is [FORMER FIELD]. The area I'm focusing in is [BROAD AREA — e.g., 'operational process' / 'organisational change' / 'regulatory and compliance work'], specifically for [CLIENT TYPE — e.g., 'smaller businesses that don't have a full in-house team for it' / 'teams going through growth or restructure']. I'm at the stage where I'm sharpening the specific offer — but the expertise is already there, I'm just deciding how to package it. Who do you know in that world right now?"*

---

**When someone seems like a potential referral source — 'could you help someone like me?'**

Do not deflect. Do not say *"I'm not quite ready yet."* Say:

> *"Tell me a bit more about what you're dealing with — I want to make sure I'm the right person before I say yes. What's the actual problem?"*

Then listen. If it connects to your background: *"Yes — this is exactly the kind of thing I'm building around. Let me follow up with you properly this week."*

If it doesn't connect: *"That's not quite in my lane, but I can probably point you somewhere useful. Can I send you a name?"*

---

### The one sentence to memorise before any networking conversation

If you remember nothing else, remember this:

> *"I'm building a consulting practice in [FORMER FIELD] and I'm currently working out the specific offer — but the expertise is there and I'm moving fast."*

Confident. True. Complete. Say it like someone who knows what they're doing — because you do.

---

### What to do after the conversation

1. **Write down the name and what they said** — even one line. This is raw data for your niche excavation work.
2. **Note any problem they described** that you could see yourself solving. Bring this into your next programme session.
3. **Follow up within 48 hours** — even just: *"Great to reconnect — I'll keep you posted as my offer takes shape."*

tools.name: The Conversation Debrief Worksheet — Turning Awkward Answers Into Niche Intelligence
tools.instructions: Complete this within an hour of any network conversation where you used one of the scripts above. One page, five questions. The answers feed directly into your Career Layer Excavation work inside the programme.
tools.content:
## After every network conversation, fill this in — it takes under 10 minutes

---

### The conversation

**Who did I speak with?**
[Name, role or context — e.g., 'former colleague from Deloitte', 'neighbour whose wife runs a small business']

**When?**
[Date]

**How did I describe what I'm doing?**
[Write the actual words you used — not what you meant to say, what you said]

---

### What happened

**Q1 — What did they ask or respond to most?**
> [Write the question or comment that made them lean in, look interested, or ask a follow-up. Even 'oh interesting, what kind of thing?' counts.]

**Q2 — What problem did they describe — even in passing?**
> [Any frustration, gap, or difficulty they mentioned related to your former field. 'We can never find anyone who understands the compliance side AND can talk to the business' counts. So does 'my team keeps stalling on these projects and I don't know why.']

**Q3 — Did any part of my answer feel true and easy to say?**
> [Mark the sentence or phrase that came out confidently — this is a signal about where your authority actually sits.]

**Q4 — Did any part of my answer feel forced, vague, or uncomfortable to say?**
> [Mark what felt like a stretch. This is not failure — it is data. Note it and bring it to your next programme session.]

**Q5 — Is there a follow-up action here?**
> [ ] Send a follow-up message by [DATE]
> [ ] Bring this conversation as an example to my next programme session
> [ ] Note this person as a potential referral source once my offer is confirmed
> [ ] Nothing needed — conversation was general

---

### Bring to the programme

At your next session or touchpoint inside the programme, share:
- The problem from Q2 (even if it felt small)
- The phrase from Q3 that felt true
- The discomfort from Q4

These three inputs are exactly what the Career Layer Excavation Process is designed to work with. You are not just networking — you are collecting evidence.

nextStep.heading: Your Next Move Inside the Programme: Bring One Real Conversation
nextStep.body: The scripts above will hold you through the three conversations that most commonly stall women before the real work begins. Now take that traction into the programme. In your first or next Career Layer Excavation session, bring one real conversation — a partner exchange, a network reconnection, or even the inner dialogue you've been having with yourself. The specific words that felt true, the problems someone described, the moment you hesitated: that is the raw material the process is built to work with. You don't need a polished niche to show up. You need one honest account of where you currently are.
